newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Wild swings cloud '97 U.S. gas forecasts.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Wild swings cloud '97 U.S. gas forecasts.

text.p: Wild swings this year in U.S. natural gas prices have made it tough on forecasters, but while 1997 promises to be just as challenging, most gas analysts agreed levels are not likely to top 1996.

"Nineteen ninety-six was a difficult year to forecast. The volatility was phenomenal, and I think we're going to have to live with more volatility next year," said Ron Barone, managing director and gas analyst at PaineWebber in New York.

Spot gas prices at Henry Hub, the NYMEX delivery point in Erath, La., which topped $4.00 per million British thermal units (mmBtu) last February, tumbled to $1.80 in September, then surged anew this month to break $4.00.
Barone, who raised his estimate once this year, expected the 1996 composite spot wellhead price to average "something north of $2.35", with projections for 1997 in the $2.05 area.
Wellhead prices typically average about 10 cents less than the pipeline price, which includes transmission costs.

"So much depends on weather, but at this point, our composite forecast for 1997 is about $2.05. However, storage is lower than I anticipated, so it could be conservative," he said, adding he was inclined to project 1997 a bit higher but still below 1996 levels.
Mike Barbis, analyst at UBS Securities in New York, said he had to revise his 1996 price projections three times.
"It definitely was a difficult year to forecast. We had a reasonably good feel for what was going to happen in natgas, but we were consistently too low," he said.
Barbis said he expected the 1996 composite spot wellhead price to average $2.35, with his 1997 estimate now at $2.10.
"Henry Hub next year may be down a little but other basins (gas producing regions) should be up," he said.

A steady winter last year drained stocks to record lows by April and storage has significantly lagged year-on-year comparisons ever since. Analysts agreed inventory concerns this year have been the driving force behind prices.

Last week's American Gas Association data showed U.S. gas inventories slipped to 75 percent of capacity and were still 214 billion cubic feet (bcf), or eight percent, below relatively low year-ago levels.
But some expected that gap to narrow significantly in coming weeks, as the rate at which it is being tapped likely will fall short of last December's weekly average of 142 bcf.

While analysts generally agreed that gas demand next year should be up by two or three percent, most expected supplies to hold steady or register only a modest gain, keeping the market balanced on a fine edge.

"It was a relatively tight supply-demand balance this year and it will probably continue at least into early next year," said Susan Bertsch, analyst at Bonner and Moore in Houston, adding things could loosen later in 1997 based on weather.

"Overall, it was a tricky year for forecasting. We started off very cold, depleted stocks, and then had to rebuild them," Bertsch said, adding 1997 prices at Henry Hub should average about 40 cents below 1996's $2.76 based on normal weather.

Analysts saw U.S. gas production next year flat to just slightly above 1996 estimates of 18.96 trillion cubic feet. And while Canadian exports rose two percent this year and helped fill the void, most expected little change in 1997.
"Canadian exports should not grow next year because of pipeline constraints," Barbis at UBS said.
